title: ESA's Juice Gains Speed During Earth Flyby Toward Jupiter
summary:
The European Space Agency's Jupiter Icy Moons Explorer, or Juice, made a close pass by Earth on September 28. It used our planet's gravity to reshape its path toward Jupiter while consuming very little fuel. This maneuver is called a gravity assist.

The carefully planned encounter changed Juice's direction by 20 degrees relative to its previous path and increased its speed by 3.5 kilometers per second. During the four weeks before the flyby, mission controllers needed only one small course correction out of six opportunities set aside. Controllers began particularly close monitoring on August 17, with intensive tracking planned to continue through October 10.

Juice reached its closest point to Earth at 13:45 CEST, or 11:45 UTC, on September 28. The spacecraft passed 8,640 kilometers above the Indian Ocean while taking a sequence of images with its monitoring cameras.

Angela Dietz, Juice's Spacecraft Operations Manager, explained that precise navigation and careful planning kept fuel use low. Using only a small amount of the propellant reserved for this flyby leaves more available for observations of Jupiter's icy moons.

Changing the spacecraft's path was the primary purpose of the flyby. The encounter also gave the mission team a chance to test Juice's science instruments using a real planetary target. This was the third such opportunity during the mission. The first came during Juice's 2024 lunar-Earth gravity assist, followed by observations of Comet 3I/ATLAS in 2025.

ESA teams spent months coordinating with the outside groups responsible for Juice's 10 scientific instruments. They scheduled instrument activities to make the most of the spacecraft's limited time and resources.

Juice project scientist Claire Vallat, who led the effort, explained that the journey offers few opportunities to calibrate and validate instruments under well-understood conditions. Calibration helps check and adjust measurements, while validation checks whether instruments work as expected.

Vallat noted that activities sometimes needed priority decisions. For example, Juice relied on battery power alone while in Earth's shadow. During the flyby, the team prioritized calibration activities relevant to work at Jupiter. They also considered whether an opportunity was unique or could be scheduled later.

Juice is scheduled to carry out 35 flybys of Jupiter's large moons Ganymede, Callisto and Europa. Discussions about instrument operations for the Europa encounters began about 10 years ago and will continue until the spacecraft passes that moon in the early 2030s.

Earth served as a rehearsal for these more demanding encounters. Scientists could check how the instruments behave in space and refine tools for analyzing future data. Juice also spent several days traveling through Earth's magnetotail, the long extension of its magnetic field that stretches away from the Sun.
why_it_matters: Saving propellant and checking instruments during the Earth encounter helps prepare Juice to gather scientific information during its planned flybys of Jupiter's icy moons.
